section_summary: This section completes a 1936 consular analysis of the South Manchuria Railway Company’s finances and reproduces its balance sheet, debt tables, operating results, and subsidiary holdings. It then documents the company’s October 1936 reorganization, including the transfer of railway functions to the Mukden-based Tetsudo Sokyoku and the creation of an Industry Department and the Manchuria Trading Company. The remainder examines the 1938–39 budget and the fiscal 1937–38 balance sheet, emphasizing railway construction for strategic purposes, wartime profits, dependence on debentures, investment in Manchukuo State Railways, and increasing subordination to the Kwantung Army.

subfiles.title: Comment on the Balance Sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year 1935–36
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the South Manchuria Railway Company’s finances, investments, debts, political role, and prospects after the establishment of Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion calculates that the company had advanced hundreds of millions of yen for Manchukuo railways while carrying substantial unpaid interest and a growing debt burden. It contrasts the company’s nominal status as a profit-making corporation with its use as an instrument of Japanese national and military policy. The despatch also discusses proposed railway and industrial reorganization, pressure from the Kwantung Army, the company’s continuing need for private capital, and President Matsuoka’s stated preference for commercially sound expansion.

subfiles.title: General Balance Sheet for the Year Ending March 31, 1936
subfiles.about: Presents the company’s assets, liabilities, profit-and-loss account, and disposition of net profit for fiscal 1935–36.
subfiles.summary: The statement values fixed assets, investments, current assets, loans, and advance payments and balances them against capital stock, reserves, bonds, deposits, and current liabilities. Its profit-and-loss account separates the results of railways, hotels, harbors, collieries, oil distillation, local administration, general operations, and interest. It also records dividends, reserve allocations, bonuses, depreciation, and the balance carried forward.

subfiles.title: Outstanding Debentures of the South Manchuria Railway Company Issued Between 1917 and 1936
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure
subfiles.about: Tabulates the company’s outstanding debenture issues as of March 31, 1936.
subfiles.summary: Degraded table of South Manchuria Railway debentures issued 1917-1936, totaling about 707.4 million yen outstanding.

subfiles.title: Comparative Business Revenue and Expenditure, Fiscal Years 1929–30 to 1935–36
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure
subfiles.about: Compares several years of revenue and expenditure for the company’s principal enterprises.
subfiles.summary: The multi-page table gives annual figures for railways, harbors and wharves, collieries, oil distillation, hotels, local administration, interest, general expenses, depreciation, and net profit. Although portions are heavily corrupted by OCR, it shows the growth of both operating income and expenditure through fiscal 1935–36.

subfiles.title: List of Subsidiary Companies and Affiliated Enterprises of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure
subfiles.about: Lists subsidiary and affiliated companies with their establishment dates, authorized capital, paid-up capital, and railway-company investment.
subfiles.summary: Table of South Manchuria Railway subsidiaries and affiliates in industry, chemicals, mining, agriculture, forestry, transport, construction, power, finance and insurance, with year established and capitalization, though many names are obscured, and notes on currencies and exchange.

subfiles.title: New Organization of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the organizational changes imposed on the South Manchuria Railway Company in October 1936.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies the offices remaining at Dairen, including the President’s Office, Finance and Accounts Department, Central Laboratory, purchasing organization, and overseas offices. Railway departments were transferred to Mukden and combined with Manchukuo State Railways and the Direction of North Chosen Railways in the Tetsudo Sokyoku. A new Industry Department absorbed research and development bodies, while the sales organization became the Hsinking-based Manchuria Trading Company.

subfiles.title: Schedule Briefing the October 1936 Changes Made in the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.about: Summarizes which company bodies remained, were reorganized, or were transferred to new organizations.
subfiles.summary: The schedule lists continuing departments and the components gathered into the new Dairen-based Industry Department under Sakatani. It separately identifies the railway bodies moved to Mukden and incorporated into the Tetsudo Sokyoku. The sales section’s transfer to the Manchuria Trading Company at Hsinking is also recorded.

subfiles.title: Department of State Reference Note on Dairen Despatch No. 20
subfiles.about: Directs attention to the translated South Manchuria Railway budget and the financing discussion in Dairen’s despatch of May 17, 1938.
subfiles.summary: Reference note on Dairen Despatch 20 on the company's budget for the year ending March 31, 1939; examine the translated budget and the newspaper-derived financing plan on pages seven and eight.

subfiles.title: Budget of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ending March 31, 1939
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Analyzes the company’s 1938–39 enterprise and operating budgets and explains its proposed financing arrangements.
subfiles.summary: The company planned enterprise spending of about 236 million yen, dominated by new and improved Manchukuo railways whose strategic value to the Kwantung Army exceeded their immediate economic rationale. Turner reviews special industrial projects, transfers of subsidiary shares to the Manchuria Heavy Industry Development Company, and projected operating profits. The despatch explains how government share calls, reserves, bank syndicate loans, public bureaus, and 170 million yen in debentures were expected to finance the program despite public distrust of the company’s military subordination.

subfiles.title: Translation: Budget of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ending March 31, 1939
subfiles.about: Provides the translated official budget approved by the Japanese Government on March 16, 1938.
subfiles.summary: Translated 1938-39 South Manchuria Railway budget: enterprise spending for ordinary company work, special industrial projects and outside investments, itemizing Showa Steel, Fushun power and coal, oil, new railways and related companies, with comparative tables of revenue, expenditure and surplus.

subfiles.title: Balance Sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year Ended March 31, 1938
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Evaluates the company’s fiscal 1937–38 balance sheet, operating results, capital program, and financial exposure to Japanese imperial policy.
subfiles.summary: Turner reports assets and liabilities of roughly 2.243 billion yen and analyzes fixed assets, investments in Manchukuo State Railways, debentures, borrowings, and current accounts. Railway traffic, military movements, and a premium on transferred subsidiary shares helped produce a record profit of nearly 74 million yen, while collieries, harbors, oil production, local administration, and interest produced mixed results. The despatch stresses investor anxiety over strategic railway construction, North China projects, Army control, and the company’s inability to obtain materials under wartime controls despite its underlying profitability.

subfiles.title: Appendix to Despatch No. 47: Financial Tables for Fiscal 1937–38
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Supplies detailed tables supporting the consular analysis of the company’s 1937–38 accounts.
subfiles.summary: The appendix contains a balance sheet, profit-and-loss and business-revenue accounts, disposition of profits, fixed-asset schedules, development expenditures, and particulars of debenture issues. It also lists railway, harbor, mining, industrial, medical, and administrative works undertaken during the year, including several projects at Fushun, Dairen, Mukden, Hsinking, and Rashin. The final tables trace share prices from 1936 to 1938, calls on government and public shares, and totals for shareholders and employees.

subfiles.title: General Balance Sheet for the Year Ending March 31, 1938
subfiles.about: Introduces the company’s formal general balance sheet for fiscal 1937–38.
subfiles.summary: These pages are the title leaves of the official balance sheet presented to the thirty-seventh General Meeting of Shareholders on June 20, 1938. They identify the reporting period and the South Manchuria Railway Company’s headquarters at Dairen; the financial tables continue beyond this section.
